newsitem.title: USA: Alaska enacts bill to spur North Slope gas project.
newsitem.headline: Alaska enacts bill to spur North Slope gas project.

text.p: Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles on Thursday signed a bill that authorizes the state to set up a cabinet-level team to negotiate tax and royalty incentives for a huge North Slope liquefied natural gas project.
The team will include the state Attorney General Bruce Botelho, Natural Resources Commissioner John Shively and Revenue Commissioner Wilson Condon.
A project to sell Alaska's estimated 35 trillion cubic feet of North Slope natural gas is much desired by state officials and residents, Knowles, the bill's sponsor, said.

"If we could just make it happen by a stroke of a pen, it would have happened a long time ago," said Knowles, a Democrat. "How we make it commercially viable in a competitive world is a different issue."

The commercialization team was directed by the bill to help find a way to reduce the estimated $15 billion cost of building a pipeline to ship North Slope natural gas to port for shipments to Asian markets.

The bill authorizes the three cabinet members to negotiate tax and royalty concessions with oil producers. Those provisions for confidential negotiations were the subject of much controversy, the governor admitted.

But without guarantees of confidentiality, North Slope oil producers -- who would also produce the natural gas -- would have "no basis" for disclosing proprietary information to the state, Knowles said.
Such disclosure "gives the state the information it needs to strike the best bargain for Alaska," he said.
The team is expected to report its findings to the governor and legislature in January, when possible incentive legislation can be drafted.
If there are any tax or royalty concessions proposed, they would have to be cleared by the legislature to be enacted, said Shively, who was at Knowles' signing ceremony.
"We can't make a deal in secret and have it be a deal," he said. "There has to be public review."

The proposed Alaska gasline project would represent the largest privately funded capital project in U.S. history, Knowles said, but it would compete with proposed gas projects from other parts of the world.
Although Alaska has vast natural gas reserves, but they remain off the market because of distances to the remote North Slope.
